title: The Jesuits suppressed (1773)
hookLine: the pope dissolves the Jesuits under political pressure; they are restored in 1814

cards: What happens to an order when the pope himself shuts it down?
In a cell in the Castel Sant'Angelo, the old fortress by the Tiber in Rome, sits an elderly priest, Lorenzo Ricci, superior general of the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits, the order Ignatius founded.
Except the order he leads no longer exists. The pope has dissolved it. Its houses are closed, its schools taken from it, its priests scattered.
Ricci is questioned, kept in custody, and never released. He dies a prisoner. Today, how an order of teachers and missionaries came to this.

teach.b: First, the kings. The decisive pressure didn't come from outside the Church. It came from Catholic courts.

Portugal, France and Spain had already thrown the Jesuits out of their lands and seized their property, for tangled reasons: politics, money, quarrels over missions and schools, resentment of the order's influence.
Then those courts pressed the pope to finish the job everywhere. Second, the pen. Pope Clement the Fourteenth gave way.
He signed a brief, known by its opening Latin words, Dominus ac Redemptor, the Lord and Redeemer, dissolving the Society for the sake of the peace of the Church. It gave no verdict of heresy.
In country after country, Jesuits laid down their order's name. They obeyed. Third, the thread that didn't break.
In the Russian Empire, Catherine the Great refused to publish the brief, so it never took effect there, and a small group of Jesuits quietly carried on. Fourth, restored.
Decades later, Pope Pius the Seventh restored the Society of Jesus for the whole Church.
The same Church that dissolved them brought them back, and the thread from Russia was part of what was rewoven.
Saint Paul knew seasons like this.

teach.h: CAST DOWN, BUT WE PERISH NOT.
teach.b: In Second Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken; we are cast down, but we perish not." Unfair seasons are real. So, in this story, are restorations.

how: Jesuits today remember the suppression and restoration as part of their own story, and their schools, parishes and retreat houses often tell it to students and retreatants as a lesson in obedience and endurance.

games.q: you're a Jesuit. the pope's brief arrives: your order no longer exists. what do you do?
o: defy the pope and keep the order going in secret.
obey, lay down the order's name, and keep serving as you can.
games.why: the Jesuits obeyed. outside Russia, they laid down their order's name and served as they could, until a later pope restored them.

practice: Bring to mind something unfair you're living with, at work, at home, in your body, in a decision someone else made, and name it plainly, without exaggerating or shrinking it.

Then ask what the Jesuits in Russia had to ask: what one small thing can I keep doing faithfully, right here? If you pray, place the whole season in God's hands; if not, let yourself hold it without hurrying it.

wordCard.voice: Lorenzo Ricci. The last superior general before the pope dissolved the Jesuits, kept in custody at the Castel Sant'Angelo, who died a prisoner.

carryVoice: Your line: restored. The story didn't end where the brief was signed. See you tomorrow.
